Psychoanalysis. A psychological theory and therapeutic method pioneered by Sigmund Freud, emphasizing the role of the unconscious mind, repressed conflicts, and early childhood experiences in shaping personality and behavior.

Freud posited that the unconscious mind harbors repressed desires, traumatic memories, and instinctual drives called libido that influence behavior, dreams, and personality development outside conscious awareness. The psychoanalytic method involves free association, speaking without censorship, and dream analysis, analyzing symbolic content to access unconscious material and resolve internal conflicts through catharsis and insight.

Psychosexual development theory proposes that personality develops through childhood stages: oral, anal, phallic, latency, and genital. Fixations at early stages cause later neurosis and character types. The Oedipal complex is Freud's most famous and criticized concept, wherein children harbor unconscious desires for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent. Defense mechanisms are unconscious psychological strategies—repression, projection, denial, sublimation, rationalization—that protect the ego from anxiety and unacceptable impulses by distorting reality.

Later psychoanalysts like Carl Jung, Alfred Adler, and Karen Horney modified Freud's framework while preserving the emphasis on unconscious processes and talk therapy. Jung emphasized the collective unconscious and archetypes. Modern neuroscience has challenged psychoanalytic theory's empirical basis. Contemporary psychoanalysis has repositioned itself as a philosophical perspective on meaning-making rather than as a scientific account of mental mechanisms. Despite criticisms, psychoanalytic concepts permeate Western culture. Freudian slips, defense mechanisms, and the talking cure remain influential in popular psychology, literature, and art.
